utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Have the accused brought in, please, Mr. Registrar. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good afternoon to the interpreters and to the steno-typists. Does everybody hear me? Good afternoon to Defence and Prosecution counsel. Good afternoon to the accused. I believe we can now continue. We're going to be here until 6.00. Let me turn to the Defence counsel for the introduction of the next witness. Will it be Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The next witness will have a pseudonym, "DJ." He is a farmer, an agricultural worker, without much education. He lived in his village throughout his life. At the start, I would like us to go into private session for a few moments for me to be able to explain where his house was and which village he lived in. He's going to describe his property, the land he owns, and his experience from the first conflict in January 1993 when he left his house for a short time, for 24 hours. After that, he's going to describe what happened in April 1993 when the Bosnia-Herzegovina army came to his village, took away all the men, took them to a prison, how they behaved to the prisoners in the prison, the injuries he sustained, the conditions during his detention, trench digging, the exchange of prisoners, and his departure for Kiseljak. He's going to describe what happened to his house. He is going to describe how many Croats lived in the village before and how many live in it today and what happened to the neighbouring villages populated by the Croats. We're going to try and be as brief as possible and to be as effective and efficient as possible. Perhaps I'll ask a few more questions than I usually do, so I'll leave the witness less time for independent talk, and I'll be asking him more shorter questions, if you agree with that kind of work. We expect to finish in 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First question, we will move to a private session. I don't have a summary. I can't find it. I have three of them. I'm not going to state the names. Was there a written summary, Mr. Dubuisson? I'm sorry. I think I'm the one who lost my copy. The second question or comment is sometimes I would like to have a narrative of the testimony, but what I've often seen is that when there are questions and answers, which one sees in purely common law systems, time is wasted. Sometimes it's true that it can be better. I do recognise that. I have confidence in you. I will not hesitate to intervene if you go into too many details. Don't go into too many funnel-like questions, but go directly to what you're asking the witness to tell you. Ask your questions concisely; otherwise, we're going to waste time. If you have any way of saving time, I would agree with that method. We can now go into a closed session. I think it would be best to have a closed session now. Will a private session be enough, Mr. Nobilo? Is a private session enough or does it have to be a closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I think that that will be sufficient. A private session will do very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objections from the Prosecution? Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we're not going to mention the place that you lived in anymore, and we're not going to mention names. We're just going to say "your village." That's the term we're going to use. Tell me now, on the 23rd of January, 1993, what happened in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in my village, in the morning at 6.00, the Muslims set up a barricade by Andric's house, and I was seeing to the livestock there. There was shooting down below. There was shooting, and some women came and told us that we had to withdraw. My father said, "Well, where are we going to go? How can we withdraw?" And he said, "Yes, refugees are already coming in from Gusti Grab, and a lot of people are being killed there already. We will have to flee as well so that they don't kill us." In the evening, at 6.00 in the evening that day, it was 6.00, and we started across the hills.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the morning at 6.00, you arrived at the Kiseljak municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Brestovsko, down by the church. It is three and a half kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you return to your house?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted) My wife, and my daughter went up there, and my father remained in the house, but he refused to leave because he said, "I'm going to stay here," and they didn't do anything to him, but they stormed our house. They made a lot of mess but didn't do anything to him. (redacted). They took what they needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean they took goods from your shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They took what they needed. We left. My father stayed down below. As I went to my daughter's that day, I returned the following day. I returned to my home the following day to see to the livestock. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: went back. On the second night, I went away once again, and I came back to see to my livestock and the pigs, and then all three of us returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So nothing happened to anybody, nothing happened to the house? Just the goods from the shop were taken; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (No audible answer)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're now going to concentrate on April 1993 when it was Easter. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to us, in April 1993, around about Easter, whether, in your village, the HVO existed? Were there any HVO units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there weren't. Of course not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they were there, who was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Muslim army was there. Yes, the army was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened during Easter?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the women left for church to hear mass, who came to the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They went to the church, the women, but the BH army came to the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when my wife had left to go to church, they came to the three of us, my father, myself, and my

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they ask you to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They asked us not to leave the house, and they ordered my father to go to the shed and to take the sheep into the shed, and they sent ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what "Mali Raj" means? Would you explain to the Court what there was in the Mali Raj and the gasworks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Mali Raj is a cafe. It's a cafe nearby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they collected all the male Croats there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There are about 15 or 18 of them. They were all older. Some of them were 70 years old. My father was born in 1912,(redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were held in the gasworks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were about 60 of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they say? Why did they collect you civilians? Why had they rounded you all up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we didn't want to go. I don't know why they rounded us up. I really can't say. I'm asking myself that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness DJ, when you answer, this is the Presiding Judge of the Court speaking to you, please look at the Judges. When you answer, look at the Judges. You turn to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well. Well, this is the first time that I'm in a court of law, so I apologise. I don't really know what's expected of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure you're not used to this. Make some effort.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't had the habit of doing this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we're concentrating on the gasworks where there were about 60 people. Were there some prisoners of war there, HVO soldiers, or were they all civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of them were civilians, except that there were younger ones too, Your Honours, yes, yes, younger people too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what were the conditions like in the gasworks? Did you have a blanket, a bed, a shower?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing, Your Honours, nothing. I slept under the manager's desk. We didn't have any showers or beds. I slept on a little blanket, and there were 60 of us there. We were afraid that we would suffocate, because there were people up to the age of 70 there with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, was there any trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the younger ones went to dig trenches, and we older ones didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, these younger men, did they go to dig trenches every day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, not every day. It would change. One day they would go and the other day they wouldn't go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But somebody went every day; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Somebody went every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court where the trenches were dug?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you. Your Honours, trenches were dug at Gunjace, Badnje, Majna, Kobiljaca, and Brestovsko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that where the front-line was, where they were digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's where the front-line was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please bring your chair up closer and speak into the microphone? Right. Would you tell the Court, the civilians who were in the gasworks and in Mali Raj, were all of them Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, all of them were Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about UNPROFOR and the Red Cross, did they come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honours. UNPROFOR came. There were two of them who were black and blue and who couldn't be brought out into the yard, but the rest of us were taken out into the yard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me. You said that you were black and blue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. Those two guys who stayed back in the offices where we slept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, were you taken out of the gasworks, out of the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why? Tell us why. How did this happen? Tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, this is the way it happened: They took us out of the gasworks and I was supposed to go and feed my cattle at home, and I did that. When I fed my cattle, they took me into my house and said, "Admit where your radio station is." And I said, "Oh, come on, I'm illiterate. How do I know what a radio station is?" And I said, "I don't have any bad feelings about anybody in this village." I don't know what he had in his hands or on his belt, I don't know, but he started beating me on the shoulders and, to tell you the truth, he said, "Confess. Where is your radio station?" I said, "What do you mean, radio station? I don't have a radio station. I never had a radio station." Well, then they picked me up and they said, "Come on. Get into the car." I got into the car, and they said that I should lie down -- I mean, in the back seat of the Stojadin car and they took me to the gasworks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you manage to see (redacted) or your father on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The next day, when they took me again to feed my cattle, it was another group of policemen who took me, and I asked this policeman, who was a nice guy, and I said, "Look, I've got to see my father and my brother. I should see them, really." And then he took me there to Mali Raj. I said, "They'll kill me. They'll kill me. There's no way I can stay alive because they keep telling me that I have this radio station."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: All right. We'll stop for a moment at this point, and I would like a document to be distributed but I would like it to remain under seal because it contains the name of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D428, and we will not put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at this. Is this a photocopy of the Red Cross card that you gave me when I first saw you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. This is what the Red Cross gave to you when they came to see you in prison; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how much time did you spend in gaol? On what date did they arrest you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this Easter holiday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is to say, the 18th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, 1993, and I was released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was released on the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did that happen? Were you released or were you exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, UNPROFOR came and then the Red Cross came and then they registered all of us, Your Honours, and then -- and then we stayed there until the 1st of May, and on the 1st of May, there was an exchange. UNPROFOR came and Vehbija Karic and some other guys from the BH came. Three or four of them; I don't know. I just know that they were addressing Vehbija Karic, and I don't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I live out there in Radanovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The municipality of Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the municipality of Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how many Croats lived in Bilalovac until the 18th of April, 1993, according to your estimate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you know, on the 28th of January, all of us fled from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But then you came back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Part of them came back, but then some of them whose houses were destroyed did not come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So let's go back to January. Until this conflict between the BH army and the HVO in January, how many Croats lived in Bilalovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, there were about 100 Croat households, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Bosnia, how many members does a Croat household have, on average? Some people have larger families, some have smaller, but on average?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it depends. (redacted) (redacted). So see what kind of difference this is? Some have more, some have less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we say that in Bilalovac, there were about 400 to 500 Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, possibly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Judges how many Croats are in Bilalovac today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, four or five, I think. Not more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Four or five men, people, or four or five households?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four or five households, and all of them elderly people at that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The villages surrounding Bilalovac, tell me, where did the Croats live around Bilalovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They lived in Kazagici, in Kazagici, Gunjace, and -- what's the name of this other place? -- Mirosevici, Sajinovici, and all these places around the gasworks. There were hardly any Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were only Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about those villages nowadays? Are there Croats living there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, there's no one. There are only destroyed and burned and looted houses. Everybody's gone to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you say that all these Croat houses were looted and destroyed; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing, Your Honours, nothing whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your machinery and everything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of it stayed up there. After this exchange on the 1st of May, everything, everything, Your Honours, remained up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you visit your house recently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when we had a memorial service at the cemetery about 15 days ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see your machinery there? Is it there or is it not there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there is nothing up there, nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All of it was taken away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of it was taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your livestock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing. Nothing, Your Honours, nothing left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does the house look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It doesn't look like anything at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, describe to us what you mean by "nothing at all."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, everything has been destroyed, more or less. The bath has been -- all the rubble lying about everywhere, there's water everywhere. Everything is open now so the water and rain can fall in and, Your Honours, everything has been destroyed and lies in ruins.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the roofs on your buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there are no roofs. Just a little bit of roof is left on the house, but the rain falls in and -- everything has been destroyed, and if I go back there, I don't have anywhere to go back to, so that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, is there anybody living in your house now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, three people, but when I visited recently, when I went to the graveyard, I found an old man living there. He was an invalid, he just had a little fire going, he didn't have a stove or anything like that. That's what it looks like, it was just a little fire that he had built up. He told me -- I said that I was the owner of the house, and he said, "Well, that's all right, young man." He looked at me and I said that "I have just come to have a look at the house," and he said, "Well, just feel free to look around. I have got nothing left myself and I'm just here --" and I placed a light bulb for him so that he at least had a little bit of light to see in the dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your son's house? There are people living there as well, aren't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there are. I didn't go into my son's house, but there are two people living there now because it was a new house, Your Honours. My house was a little older, built a little earlier on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court, please, while you were in Kiseljak as a refugee during the war in 1993, did you dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, I did. When I was in a good state of health, I signed up for trench-digging. I am a physical labourer so I'm used to working physically. I can't just sit around doing nothing. And I dug trenches around Bileca, Majna, Gunjace, Brestovsko, around those parts, Kazagici. That's where it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it up by the front-lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was by the front-lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who dug trenches with you? Croats or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We Croats, Your Honours, dug the trenches. There were no Muslims where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, this concludes our examination-in-chief. We would just like to tender in evidence this Defence Exhibit and we request that it remain under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. The exhibit will be tendered. This is still in public session. I think that Mr. Kehoe will conduct the cross-examination. Witness DJ, you will now be asked questions by the Office of the Prosecutor, he will ask for some clarifications, and you may be asked some questions by the Judges, and then everything will be over, unless there is re-examination by the Defence. Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can go into private session just briefly and I will be done quite quickly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objections, I suppose? All right. Private session for a very short time. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Mr. DJ, we're from the Office of the Prosecutor, and we just want to say sorry for your troubles. We have no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Re-examination? I suppose there isn't going to be one since there were no questions asked by the Prosecutor. It would be logical, I suppose, that there is nothing for you to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No, the Defence has no reason for additional questions, and we're happy to see that the Prosecutor can feel for this man, and if an indictment would come out of this, it would be even better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Riad, do you have any questions, or Judge Shahabuddeen? I don't have any questions either. We thank you very much. It was relatively quickly done. You have gone through very painful experiences, and we hope that as time goes by you will find serenity again. The Tribunal thanks you very, very much. The usher is now going to accompany you out of the courtroom. Thank you once again. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There is some preparation needed. We are going to take a five-minute break, but this is not the real break. I say that for the sake of the interpreters. Just a five-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing will now resume. We will now resume with a public session, but the witness is protected. I turn to him -- since the witness is covered by protective measures, he can answer without any fear. First, identify yourself, please. Do not move. Identify your name on the piece of paper which the registrar is showing you and simply nod if, in fact, the name is yours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Nods)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Judges will allow you to remain seated while you take your oath. You will be given a text by the usher, and we ask that you read it out loud. Your voice has been altered; is that not correct, Mr. Registrar? Is the voice distorted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You have come to the Tribunal, and we thank you for doing so, at the request of the Defence in the trial of General Blaskic, who is today a General and is accused by the International Criminal Tribunal. You may speak without hatred, without fear and in full sincerity and serenity under the protection of the Tribunal. After Mr. Nobilo asks you his questions, you will be asked questions by the Prosecution and perhaps the Judges will have some questions to ask you as well, but we will decide that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Speak "without" fear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Without fear, without hatred, without any fear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Speak "without" fear, not "about" fear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: "Without," yes. Thank you, Judge Riad. Yes. I think that we can begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to have a map distributed at the very outset. It also has a legend. So could you please have both distributed? Please put a copy on the ELMO. The original is somewhat bigger than those copies that all the participants will receive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will delay the break for a little while, if the interpreters agree. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D429, 429 for the caption, and I would like to say that this is a confidential document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No. It is not under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, could we please move into private session only for a few moments so that we could talk about this witness, and then we are going to move into public session immediately, please? (Private session)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Witness DK, could you please take the pointer over there, and then please look at the small map that is over there on the left-hand side on the ELMO. Could you please show me where Busovaca is and then please show us the road that leads to Gusti Grab where you lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Busovaca (indicating), Gusti Grab (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How many kilometres away is Gusti Grab from Busovaca in the direction of Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Exactly six kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell the Court, when did you join the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: I joined the HVO at the beginning of 1992 as I lost my job at the steelworks in Zenica. These units were being established, and so I spontaneously joined the HVO unit, just like everybody else did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This HVO unit that you joined, who was in this unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Mostly people from my village, mostly peasants who worked in the Zenica steelworks until then and in other companies in that area. Most of the people were involved in agriculture, and they did not have any military skills. Nobody had been in a military unit before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How did you get a commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: We chose one of our own. We chose a man whom we trusted. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please tell the Court, when you joined the HVO, what did you do then? What duties did you have? Did you go somewhere? What did you do in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: At the beginning when the unit was organised, we didn't go anywhere. We patrolled our own village during 1992. In mid 1992, we started going to Jajce, to the defence lines vis-à-vis the Serb units. After that, we went to Paklarevo, a village near Travnik on Mount Vlasic, the slopes of Mount Vlasic. We had defence lines over there, again, vis-à-vis the Serb units and vis-à-vis the former JNA units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So those were your duties, patrolling in your village and also going to the front-line against the Serbs. Tell me, what was your relationship like with your neighbours, the local Muslims, throughout 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: As I already said, the village of Gusti Grab is surrounded on all sides by villages that were populated by Muslims. However, our relations with the Muslims were very good. Before the war, we used to work together, and there was some cooperation in agricultural work, and we worked together in the factory, and our children went to school together, so our relations were very good indeed. However, as the people from Krajina came in from Banja Luka, Prijedor, Prnjavor, the Muslims from there who were expelled by the Serbs, as they came to Bosnia, to Zenica, to Kakanj, also a lot of them came to Kacuni, to my village too, well, then there was growing tension.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before you move on further, could you show the Court where Kacuni is in relation to Gusti Grab, your village, where the people from Krajina came who fled from the Serbs? What are you showing us now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: That's Kacuni (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Your village, where was the centre where these people from Krajina were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Their seat, rather, was in the former JNA barracks and also in a building which was called "silos." That was actually one kilometre away from Kacuni. This is a massive concrete building which was used for storing wheat before, so it was really a storage space for wheat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When did these people come from Krajina, these new Muslims who fled from the Serbs, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: They came at the end of October, the beginning of November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What changed then? Could you describe it to the Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Many changes took place then. As I said, until then, our relations with the local Muslims were very good. However, as these people from Krajina came in, the situation changed radically. Provocations started. There was even shooting. Roadblocks were set up on the Busovaca-Kiseljak road. The Croat population was mistreated practically at every step, because people were frightened and the situation became tense, as the people from Krajina came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did this have a negative effect on the Croats, on the overall relationship between the Croats and the Muslims? What did the Croats think about these people from Krajina? Why did they come there precisely?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Please say "question" and "answer." This is to the interpreters. Please say "question" and "answer." Otherwise, we cannot follow it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: These people were expelled by the Serb units. At first, the Croats understood their position, and they were welcome, but as they came, the situation changed radically. People were afraid. There were everyday provocations, as I said, and there was panic. They were afraid. They lived in fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please describe to the Court what happened on the 24th of January, 1993, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: On the 24th of January --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Please say "question" and "answer." We can't follow it this way.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: On the 24th of January, 1993, on the road between Busovaca and Kiseljak, the first armed incident occurred. The people from Krajina, whom I already mentioned, set up roadblocks on the road between Busovaca and Kiseljak. They controlled the traffic, and, in the meantime, an HVO vehicle came by, and it was moving from Busovaca to Kiseljak. However, it was stopped at the existing roadblock, and there was an ambush placed there, and fire was opened against this vehicle. A Zolja rocket was fired then. It missed. However, fire was also opened from automatic weapons, and Ivica Petrovic was killed on that occasion, a member of the military police of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the 24th of January, 1993, there was shooting in the vicinity of your village. What did you and the other men from the village, who comprised the HVO unit, do? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: After the armed incident, which occurred on the 24th of January, the afternoon, the remainder of the day and night were peaceful. However, the next day, at the defence line which we had at the position of Mount Vlasic ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When did you put this defence line on Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: After the people from Krajina arrived, that is to say, in October and November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Why there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: That is the dominant position which was above the village, and we thought that we could defend ourselves the best from there, so it was a dominant quota.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So it was a hill. Could you please show the Court now where these defence trenches of yours were and what is the number showing them on this map? Tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Quota 641.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How is it marked on the map? How did we mark it, with which number?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So it is position number one, and that is where you had your defence line. However, when the shooting started and when Petrovic was killed, when, in fact, did you personally go up to this hill?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: I went to this hill on the 24th in the evening after the incident that occurred on the road between Busovaca and Kiseljak, after the Petrovic incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How many of you gathered up there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Forty-five members of the HVO from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell the Court what happened the next day on the 25th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: The 25th of January, 1993, at 6.00 in the morning, an all-out attack against our defence line took place at the Vlasic quota. The attack came from the directions depicted as 2, 3, and 9 on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you show the Court on the map the directions of attack at daybreak in the morning, and tell us from what villages they attacked your positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: At daybreak on the 26th in the morning, the first attacks began from the village of Bozevici, Mihaljevici, Kozlovici, Podbare, and Dolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: These are arrows numbered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: As 2, 3, and 9. Those were attacks on the 26th in the morning -- on the 25th in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How long did you manage to hold this point of defence while defending your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: We managed to hold out throughout that day on the 25th until the evening, and then we knew that we couldn't stay there very long, so we decided to evacuate the civilian population, old people, women, and children, so we did that. On the 25th in the evening, we waited for night to fall, and then we decided to pull the elderly, women, and children out of the village, so we did it along parallel lines along the Busovaca-Kiseljak road. The road was already held by members of the BH army then, so we couldn't do this along the road, but we had to do it in the hills during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court, before we move on to this evacuation of civilians, were you attacked from the other side too on the 25th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes. In the afternoon on the 25th of January, the attack came from the other side too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you describe which villages, and could you show on the map which directions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Arrows 4, 5, 6, 7, and 10, and the villages, Mehurici, Podastinje, Zecica, Vukeljici, Botun, Maj and Vladici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So the arrows show the directions of the attack, and circle number 10 shows the silos where the seat of the people from Krajina were; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: At what time did you send the refugees towards Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: This was in the evening, around 5.00 p.m. Night was already falling, and we decided to evacuate civilians. However, until then, there had been civilian casualties, which sped up our decision to evacuate the civilians. Unkica Basipa (phoen) was killed before that by a sniper in front of her home. In the neighbouring village of Oseliste, which is a village next to Gusti Grab, we found out about this the next day, there were four civilians casualties, Miko Kristo, Anto Stejko, a husband and wife, Mijo and Anje Grubisic too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, on the map, what numbers are the arrows showing where the civilians were moving out of Gusti Grab and then Oseliste?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Number 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The village belongs to the municipality of Busovaca. Could you tell us why you fled to Kiseljak rather than Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: We decided on the direction of Kiseljak because, at that time, in Kiseljak, there was still not any fighting, so we considered that that was better, because in Busovaca, the whole of that day, there was fighting, as was fighting in our area. That is why we decided upon Kiseljak as our direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: These civilians fled and withdrew parallel to the road. Can you tell us how many civilians at that time moved in the column towards Kiseljak, to the best of your assessment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: There were 70 to 80 of them, women, children, and mostly elderly men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there any shooting at them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where did the shooting come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: From the direction of the villages that I mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell us the numbers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Numbers 2, 3, and 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you explain to the Court, please, the civilians left, fled, and what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: After the civilians had left and we gave them a two-soldier escort, we remained on our line, and we stayed there as much as we were able to, but the next day, we began to withdraw to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What day was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: It was Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The 26th of April, 1993; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What happened to you then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Before I decided to withdraw, I asked the commander of the front-line to go back to the village and to visit Mrs. Luca Lalic, who was a relation of mine and who remained in the village. I knew she was still there. She was 86 years old. We didn't have any possibility of taking her out of the village, so she had to stay. I asked my commander to give me permission to visit this old relation of mine to see if I could give her any assistance of any kind. I went back to the house of Mijo Patista where my old relation was living. I came up to the house. I did not notice anything fishy. I went into the house to help her. However, when I entered the house, I was ambushed by the members of the BH army, who were all around us, and I was arrested on that occasion and taken to the place silos that I mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I think I made a mistake a moment ago. It was the 26th of January, 1993, was it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before we go on to describe the events in silos, after you had become a prisoner of war, can you tell me whether some civilians stayed in your village, the village of Gusti Grab?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes, of course, just as Mrs. Lalic stayed behind, so, also, did Mrs. Ljubica Ljubicic. She remained with her invalid husband who was paralysed, so we were not able to transport him either. Marijan Cavara and Stipo Tomas remained behind, which means a total of four. Mr. Tomas stayed with his family. However, all the civilians I mentioned were killed several days after the departure of our unit from our front-line, that is to say, after our withdrawal, and all the other civilians were killed. Marijan Cavara, Stipo Tomas, Ljubica Ljubicic, and Luca Lalic, they were all killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were they older people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, Ljubica Ljubicic was 86 years old. Marijan Cavara was the youngest of them all, and he was 57 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before we continue with the events that followed, we can take a break and look at what happened to the village. First of all, how many Croat houses existed in the village of Gusti Grab?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: There were 50 to 60 Croat houses, and these houses, that is, a lesser number, were destroyed during the fighting. Some were hit by mortar fire, but, as I say, it was a smaller number of houses. The other houses were destroyed later on. After the signing of the first cease-fire, most of the houses were looted and then set fire to. A very small number of houses, which were nearer to the road between Kiseljak and Busovaca, the Muslims went to live in them, but this was a smaller number, as I say. For the most part, they were looted and burnt and left. Nobody has yet returned to Gusti Grab. As it remained that day, it remains to this present day, so none of the Croats returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The neighbouring village of Oseliste, what happened there? Was the situation similar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes, it was. What happened to that village was the same as in the other village. The houses were burnt, the population had fled, and nobody has returned to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us now go back to the 26th of January, 1993. You, yourself, as an HVO soldier, were taken to silos. Would you describe to the Court, please, the conditions of your sojourn in that facility? You said that a silo was there for storing grain. Would you describe what the building looked like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Well, it was a big concrete building, as I said, made of concrete mostly. There were 10 to 12 large, sort of, rooms, ten by five metres in size, and a little smaller rooms. This building was used by the BH army to store ammunition and weapons for the army, and a part of the command was located there as well in the silos.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The command was on an upper story. Where were you located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: I was located in a cell on the ground floor, and the dimensions were, as I have already said, ten by five metres. I was taken to this room which did not have any heating and did not have a bed. I spent the first three days imprisoned there on my own. I was by myself, and as soon as I got to the prison, I was taken for interrogation. They wanted to get information from me, the information that I just did not have. They asked me about our weapons, warehouses, ammunition, food, radio stations, heavy weaponry, which we did not have. When I was not able to tell them any of this, because I did not know anything, we didn't have any of these facilities, I was beaten up immediately on the spot. I had to stand up by the wall with my arms and legs stretched out and my forehead up against the wall, and they beat me on the back using police batons or rifle butts or with their feet and legs and anything they could find. This occurred several times in the first three days that I spent alone in my cell. On the fourth day, they transferred me to another room similar to the first room, and I found 13 other HVO members in that room, and they too had been taken prisoner by the people of Krajina. Before the fighting itself, that is to say, after the Petrovic incident, these people were taken to the silo, and on day four, I was transferred to their cell. I was together with them in the cell. On that occasion, we had to greet the Muslims coming into the cell, and we had to use their own Islamic terms of greeting, terms which they used amongst themselves, such as Merhaba, Salam Haleikoum, and I don't really know what these terms mean. When I was transferred to this second cell, they continued to maltreat me and to beat me up, but the way in which they did this changed somewhat. Usually four or five of them would enter the cell. One of them would immediately take out his gun. He would start firing, and he would turn the barrel of the gun towards my leg, and then he would warn us and threaten us, and say that nobody must try to avoid a blow or block the person hitting us. We had to sit as we were sitting, and then three or four of them made a column. They went one by one and beat us. They repeated this several times going around in a circle. We had to remain sitting. We were not able to move. We were not allowed to move. They just hit us and beat us up as they saw fit. I could also add that, on two occasions, I lost consciousness from the beatings given me by the members of the BH army. On those occasions, they took me out of the cell into another similar cell, and then in the position that I said a moment ago, with my arms stretched out and my legs stretched out and my forehead up by the wall, two or three of them would beat me with police batons until I had lost consciousness. This was repeated twice. Then they would take me back to the cell in the kind of state I was in, beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You had serious bodily injury done to you during these beatings, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes. In one of the beatings, and these beatings were repeated day after day, I got serious bodily harm. My jaw was broken. I was kicked with an army boot in my jaw, and this was a severe bodily injury. I had an open fracture of the jaw. Afterwards, I felt very strong pain, and I asked for medicines to be given to me for the pain, but I received nothing. On the occasion, they just made fun of me, and they said, "Well, you shouldn't be here anyway. You should go to Croatia. That's where you belong. This is Bosnia-Herzegovina. This belongs to the Muslims and only to the Muslims, and you're going to go away from here, so there's nothing for you here."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The people that said this to you, were they your neighbours or were they the people from Krajina that had fled in the face of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: No. They were not our neighbours. Even in prison, they were fair and correct in their conduct towards us, but the people from Krajina beat us up and they said things of this kind to us and made us use the Islamic terms of greeting that I mentioned a moment ago, and I felt that our neighbours, the Muslims, seemed to be afraid of the people from Krajina themselves, that they too were afraid of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you received these severe bodily injuries, could you describe how this happened? What position were you in and how did you sustain these injuries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: I was sitting on a wooden bench in the cell, and four or five of them entered the cell and they did what they did. One of them took a rifle and started -- a gun and started shooting. We were told not to move, that we were not allowed to move, and then they would move around in a column, one after the other, beating us any which way. They paid no attention how they struck us or where they struck us. So we were sitting down. I was in a sitting-down position when I was kicked in my jaw, and that is how my jaw was fractured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps this would be the time to take a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Shall we continue? At one point in time, did the International Red Cross come to your prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes. The International Red Cross came on the eighth or ninth day of our stay in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did they give you IDs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes. A few officials of the International Red Cross came, and Mr. Stipo Santic came with them, an official of the Red Cross from Busovaca. On that occasion, the International Red Cross registered us, gave us IDs, and also on that occasion, we got some sanitary materials which we did not have until then and we also got some cigarettes. I could also say that during our stay in prison, the hygiene was non-existent. We didn't have toilets to go to. We had to relieve ourselves in the rooms where we were staying. So it was very bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you take baths?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: No, never. Throughout our stay there in prison, there were no conditions for hygiene.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: After the Red Cross came, did the conditions improve in terms of the attitude of the BH army soldiers towards you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: No, not at all. After the International Red Cross left, everything remained the same. After that, we were beaten, mistreated. The people from Krajina said the same things as they were saying before that, that this was their land, that they would move in there, that they would throw the Croats out, that the Croats had no place there, that Croatia was for them to live in, that this was their land, that they were to decide on our fate, that they could execute us whenever they wanted to, that they would simply decide what our destiny would be. So after the International Red Cross left, our treatment in prison remained the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: However, there was an exchange, nevertheless. On what date were you exchanged and in which way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes. On the 8th of February, 1993, the exchange took place according to the principle "all for all." A bus came from Busovaca, escorted by UNPROFOR and with a few officials of the Red Cross, so there in the silos an exchange was carried out, and then we could state our views who wanted to go where. I personally went to Busovaca, my family was down there, so on the 8th of February, I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, you were shut in the silos all the time, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the map that is on the ELMO, are the silos marked with a number 10, a little circle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to have a document distributed. That is a Red Cross ID. I would like it to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D430.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: After you left, after the exchange, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: After the exchange, I went to Busovaca, and I asked for medical assistance because of the injuries sustained in prison. I had to seek medical assistance. But my injuries were of such a nature that I could not receive adequate treatment in Busovaca or the nearby hospital in Nova Bila. I was sent for medical treatment to Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We would like a new document to be introduced into evidence, please, under seal as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The photocopy that is in front of you of a Red Cross ID, is that a photocopy of the ID that we got from you, of your ID?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D431.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, these are medical documents. Unfortunately, we received this at the very last moment so we didn't manage to get it translated, but we shall do so and we take it upon ourselves. On page 2, I draw your attention to the diagnosis in Latin which is quite recognisable, and one can see that his jaw was fractured and that his nose was fractured too, and also that there were several swellings on his head. You can see this from the Latin diagnosis, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness DK, do you agree to our discussing this medical certificate, because these are your injuries; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Witness DK, tell us, this paper that you got in the hospital in Split, did you get it after you were released and during your treatment there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have thus concluded the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is there any objection to the tendering of these exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Judge. I haven't read this particular document, but -- I know it's been a few years. I can make out a little bit of the Latin myself. I don't anticipate it, Judge, but -- so at this point, if we just admit it with some reservations so I can just maybe get a rough translation of it, but I don't think there will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We congratulate you for your knowledge of the fourth official language of the Tribunal, that's Latin. Now, if you have any objections you would like to make, you can make them in a few days once the document has been translated. Perhaps you will now begin with the cross-examination. Witness DK, as I'm sure you've been told, the Office of the Prosecutor is going to ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You are an authority on Latin. Would you translate it to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can't translate it literally, Judge, but I can make out a few words here and there in order to come to the conclusion that whatever happened to this gentleman wasn't good. That's my medical diagnosis based on that first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I want to be sure that the witness understands that this is a moment of a little bit of relaxation here that we have just heard, but we are taking your condition extremely seriously and we will look at the document very seriously. Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. DK, I meant no disrespect concerning your injuries which I can see from your testimony were quite serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Witness DK, my name is Greg Kehoe. I'm from the Office of the Prosecutor. My two colleagues to my right are Mr. Mark Harmon and Mr. Andrew Cayley respectively. I would just like to ask you a couple of questions, Witness DK, and it won't be that lengthy. Witness DK, you gave us your date of birth. That was given to us in a private session, and we need not go into the specific date of birth, but did you serve in the JNA having done national service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: That was in 1977.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How long were you in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Fifteen months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Witness DK, you said you joined the HVO, I believe, sometime in 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you noted to us that you joined with many of the other men in your community; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: From my village, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, from your village. Would it be fair to say, Witness DK, that virtually all of the men that were in the HVO from your village had done national service with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Witness DK, you noted for us that you went to the front-lines in Jajce.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was that a common thing for soldiers in the JNA (sic) to do during 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: For JNA soldiers? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I misspoke. Excuse me. I apologise. Was it normal for HVO soldiers to go to the front-line at Jajce during 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How did you get to Jajce? How did you and the other HVO soldiers get to Jajce?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: We had transportation by bus from Busovaca, so we went to Jajce to defend it from the Serb units, that is to say, to the defence line vis-à-vis the Serb units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So correct me if I'm wrong, you received notification that you were supposed to go to the front in Jajce and then you got on buses with other soldiers in the HVO and they drove you to Jajce; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So this was done in an organised fashion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: One could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, could I ask you, Witness DK, just briefly to take a look at this map, I think it's Defence 429? If we could give that to the witness? Now, Witness DK, before we go into this particular map, let me just ask you another question. I neglected to note that there were other HVO units that went up to Mount Vlasic to go on the line against the Bosnian Serbs in that location also; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes, and also there were BH army units. At that time, we went together to defend the line against the Serb units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So did you do service, Witness DK, in both the Jajce area and also up on Mount Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes. I was there twice, seven days respectively. Seven days in Jajce and seven days on Mount Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you noted for us just a few moments ago that you got on a bus with other HVO soldiers that took you to Jajce. Did you follow the same procedure when you and other HVO soldiers went up to the line at Mount Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: We also went to Mount Vlasic together with the Muslim units. The organisation was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Excuse me one moment. Now, just, if I may, go back to Exhibit 429, the map that's on the ELMO, Witness DK. You noted for us that your trench line was on position 1; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I never mentioned trench-digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. I'm not talking about trenches. Can you just take a look at the map that's to your left, or maybe it's on the ELMO before you, and maybe I misheard you, Witness DK, but did you not tell us you had a defensive position at the area that is marked number 1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were there trenches, was it a trench there, or what type of defence line are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, were there other trenches along that same line that were dug by other villages such as Oseliste?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: No. At this defence line were only our trenches that we dug, we from the village of Gusti Grab. Two or three hundred metres away from ours were the trenches of the BH army. The village of Oseliste is not that close to the village of Gusti Grab, so we did not have any contact. It's a bit further away, so we did not have any contact in combat action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Witness DK, other than the trenches that you said that are at point 1, were there other HVO trenches along this line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Along the line, along our defence line, which was one and a half kilometres long, there were about ten trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Maybe I'm not being clear here, Witness DK. To the left and the right of the trenches that are designated as number 1, were there any other HVO trenches in either direction that you know of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: No, there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the particular trenches that you had up in point 1, when did you dig those?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: We dug them mostly after the people from Krajina came, the ones I mentioned, that is to say, October and November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Which way were those trenches facing? Were they facing towards the numbers 2, 3, and 9, or facing towards the numbers 4, 10, 5, and 6?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: We were facing trenches 2, 3, and 9. We did not have enough people. As I said before, there was a total of 45 of us all together. There wasn't enough of us to have a defence line at 4, 5, 6, 7, and 10, the other side. We knew this was necessary, but we simply didn't have enough manpower, so we decided on defence where numbers 2, 3, and 9 are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Witness DK, there were no lines with the Bosnian Serbs around here, were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: No, not at this location because the Bosnian Serbs are several dozen kilometres away, so there weren't any -- there weren't any Serb units that were facing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might have one moment, Mr. President? Witness DK, I'm sorry for your troubles. I hope your injuries have gotten better to some degree. Thank you very much for coming. Mr. President, Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just one, two, or three questions at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Witness DK, you said that in 1977, you were in the Yugoslav People's Army and that in 1992 you joined the HVO. Did you, in this period of 15 years, have any contact with the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: No, I did not have any contacts with the army, and in 1977, in the Yugoslav People's Army, I served in the anti-aircraft unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you went to the front towards the Serbs in Vlasic and Jajce, once Vlasic, once Jajce, was this a mobilisation, compulsory mobilisation, or was it voluntary, who turns up, turns up, who doesn't, doesn't?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it was like. If you turned up, you turned up. If not, there would be no disciplinary measures taken, so it was on a volunteer basis, and this departure to Jajce and Paklarevo, it was purely on a voluntary basis, and the lines held by the HVO at the time, together with the Muslims, were of a defensive nature. We had no combat operations, no attacks of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the discussion with your colleagues on the front, with the HVO members, was this volunteership equal with others or not? Compulsory mobilisation, did that exist anywhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: As far as I know, everything was like that. There was no mobilisation. Everything was on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that in October and November, that you started digging trenches when the people from Krajina came, and you also said that across from you, from the directions 2, 3, and 9, trenches were already dug by the BH army. When had they dug their trenches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Well, the 2, 3, and 9 positions and the trenches there were dug far before our own trenches, so they had dug these trenches in the summer of 1992 already, and I can freely state that they had much more modern positions, and the trenches that they dug were dug using earth-moving machinery and tractors. They had more modern trenches than we did, and they had dug their trenches before us. We did not think it necessary to dig trenches because, as I say, our relations with the Muslims beforehand had been very good. However, with the advent of the Krajishici people, we felt the need to dig these trenches because we were afraid of an attack with the arrival of the people from Krajina. And the Bosnia-Herzegovina army trenches, therefore, had been dug far before our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell the Court, please, the trenches that had been dug before your own trenches from the directions of 2, 3, and 9, were they turned towards the Croat villages and your own village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Riad, do you have any questions? Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, I have a question. Witness DK, the people who attacked you and treated you ill were from Krajina. They were Muslims, I take it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Previously, you had lived well, the Croats had lived well with the local Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Very good relations, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What happened with those relations during the ensuing conflict? I am talking about relations between the local Croats and the local Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Relations began to deteriorate with the arrival of the people from Krajina. Various provocations broke out such as shooting, the setting up of barricades, the roadblock along the Busovaca-Kiseljak road, and various communications were stopped. There were controls along the road. There was looting at the barricades, mostly of the Croat population, and so relationships became tense with the arrival of the people from Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: In your judgement, is there any prospect of those relations improving? Have they improved? Are they likely to improve?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Well, some measures of improvement are with us, and I truly hope that relationships return to what they were before the war. We are working on that, and some steps forward have been made, and I hope that that will be the case. I wish for it wholeheartedly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, I think I could say, Witness DK, that I share entirely your hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have only one question to ask you. When you were in the HVO, could you tell us who your chiefs were, the chief that was closest to you and then the one that you recognised as being the highest. There must have been a brigade commander. Did you know where your orders were coming from? Even if it was an army made up of villagers, there were orders telling you to do this or that. How did it work? Who were those men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: My immediate commander, my first superior, was also from my village, a man whom we had elected from amongst our ranks, amongst ourselves, as I said, at the beginning. In Busovaca, there was the Nikola Subic-Zrinski brigade. The commander of the brigade was called Mr. Dusko Grubesic. Our captain, which was known as the second platoon later on, which belonged to the 2nd Battalion, was within the formations of the Busovaca Nikola Subic-Zrinski brigade, and if we received any orders -- as I have said, we worked in our village, we had watches. We did not receive any separate orders. We did not have any military training of any kind. We were just, as I said, people living in their own homes doing their usual -- going about their usual business, and if we did get orders, this was from Busovaca from Mr. Dusko Grubesic or from Mladen Akrap who was the commander of the battalion there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mladen ... As regards the accused, in your opinion, who was he? Was he a leader that you recognised? Was he the chief?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: I did not have any views -- that is to say, I was in my village, so I did not know of the command structures and the commanders. As far as the accused is concerned, I had heard of him, but I did not know what his duties were and responsibilities. I wasn't informed of these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Since then, have you learned what his responsibilities were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: I knew that he was a commander, but I didn't know all his duties and responsibilities. I knew later on that he was the commander, but essentially I didn't know what that implied, what all his duties and responsibilities actually were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Were your comrades in that same condition, they didn't know either, that you only had an immediate superior, it was Mr. Dusko Grubesic? Was that how it was? All your comrades were like you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that the Tribunal sympathises with your injuries. We hope that you are feeling better now and that, if possible, you will be able to forget this dreadful period of your life. Now you will be taken out of the courtroom, you will be taken care of by the Victims and Witnesses Unit, and the Tribunal would like to thank you for having come to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, we were not so optimistic as to think we would get through three witnesses this evening. We have more witnesses for tomorrow, but we do not have another witness in the witness room right now. So that would conclude our presentation for this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. You see? That happens to all the parties, that is, running out of witnesses. Let me remind you of that. Having said so, we take note of what you have just said and will allow the interpreters to breathe a bit, and we will meet again tomorrow morning at 9.45 for a long morning. The hearing is adjourned. But for the time being, witness, please do not move.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
